children.label: harmony rule
children.tooltip:
harmony rule that defines which hues are considered 'in harmony'.

monochromatic: a single hue family — only one node.
analogous: three adjacent hues spaced 30° apart — naturalistic, cohesive.
analogous complementary: analogous triad plus its complement — rich but balanced.
complementary: two hues opposite on the wheel — high contrast, vibrant.
split complementary: one hue and the two hues flanking its complement — vivid yet less stark.
dyad: two hues separated by 60° — gentle contrast.
triad: three hues evenly spaced 120° apart — balanced, colorful.
tetrad: four hues in two complementary pairs spaced 60° — complex, needs restraint.
square: four hues evenly spaced 90° apart — strong and varied.
custom: define all four harmony node hues independently.

analyze the image's hue distribution and automatically suggest the harmony rule
and anchor hue that best match its existing color palette.

the detection scores every rule and anchor combination against a chroma-weighted
histogram of the preview image, then selects the combination that already covers
the most chromatic energy — i.e. requires the least correction.

the result replaces the current rule and anchor hue. use pull strength to control
how strongly the remaining off-palette colors are pulled toward the detected palette.

controls.label: pull strength
controls.tooltip:
how strongly off-harmony hues are pulled toward the nearest harmony node.

0: no effect — colors are left unchanged.
low values (0.1–0.3): subtle nudge, colors lean toward the palette without
  losing their original character.
high values (0.7–1.0): aggressive correction, most hues converge noticeably
  onto the harmony nodes.

the shift is weighted by each pixel's chroma: fully desaturated pixels (grays)
are never affected regardless of this setting.

controls.label: pull width
controls.tooltip:
controls the angular reach of each harmony node's attraction.

the attraction is Gaussian — strongest at the node center and tapering smoothly
outward. zone width scales the standard deviation of this Gaussian linearly.

narrow (< 1): only hues very close to a node are pulled — selective, precise.
  useful when colors are already near-harmonic and need only a gentle correction.
default (1): each node's influence tapers to near-zero at the midpoint between
  adjacent nodes — clean separation with smooth transitions.
wide (> 1): attraction zones overlap — broader, more global hue shift.
  useful for strongly discordant images or when a painterly look is desired.

controls.label: neutral color protection
controls.tooltip:
shields low-chroma (desaturated) colors from the hue correction.

0: no protection — grays, skin highlights, and muted tones are all shifted.
low values (0.1–0.3): only near-neutral grays are exempted; pastels are still affected.
mid values (0.4–0.6): muted and pastel colors are increasingly spared.
high values (0.7–1.0): only vivid, saturated colors are corrected; everything else
  is left close to its original hue.

the weighting is smooth and hyperbolic — there is no hard cutoff. protection grows
gradually from zero and the slider response is distributed evenly across its range.

controls.label: smoothing
controls.tooltip:
controls the intensity of smoothing applied to the correction field.

0: disable smoothing (recommended) — transitions are handled by smooth interpolation
  in hue space, preserving the maximum amount of image detail.
low values (0.1–0.5): subtle spatial averaging to reduce color noise in shadows.
high values (> 1.0): broad spatial blending; creates a soft, painterly look but may
  blur the grading across image edges, causing some visual separation.
